quiz.prompt: An account with almost no posting history comments "SCAMMER 'to, wag kayo mag-order dito" on your client's newest post. What is the strongest response?

options.text: Delete the comment immediately so it does not spread, then block the account before anyone else sees it
Reply in a long thread defending the business, answering every follow-up until the accuser runs out of things to say
Reply once in public with checkable facts, ask for the reference number so you can trace it, then stop
Ignore it completely, since replying to a scam accusation only pushes the comment into more people's feeds

quiz.explanation: Deleting hands the accuser a screenshot and a better story, and arguing keeps the thread alive at the top of the post. One calm, verifiable reply plus silence is what the onlookers judge you on.

quiz.prompt: Your client's Facebook Page has a negative recommendation you believe is unfair, and under it a comment listing another customer's full name and phone number. What does the module's rule say?

options.text: Hide both of them, since an unfair recommendation does the page as much damage as a leaked phone number does
Hide the comment carrying the personal details, leave the recommendation up, and answer it calmly in public
Leave both up and reply to each in public, since hiding anything at all can be read as censorship
Report both to the platform and wait for its decision, rather than making the call on the page yourself

quiz.explanation: Hiding is for content that exposes or harms someone: personal details, slurs, threats, scam links. A negative recommendation that is merely unfair stays up and gets a calm reply, and you agree the hide-and-delete rule with the client in writing before the night you have to use it.

quiz.prompt: You ask Claude or ChatGPT to draft a reply to a public complaint about a damaged order. What is the right way to use what it gives you?

options.text: Send whichever version sounds the most professional, since a complaint reply is urgent and speed is what matters
Send the strongest draft as written, adding the customer's name at the top so the reply feels personal
Ask the AI to decide whether a refund or a replacement is the fairer outcome here, then send that
Treat the drafts as options, cut any policy or timeline you cannot verify, and get the client's yes

quiz.explanation: AI will confidently invent refund policies and delivery timelines it has no way of knowing, and it has no idea what your client can afford. Use it for wording and tone; the decision about money and risk stays with you and the client.

quiz.prompt: Your client's page gained 900 followers this month, but inquiries dropped from 34 to 19. What goes at the top of your one-page report?

options.text: The drop in inquiries, the likely reason for it, and the three things you will change next month
The follower growth, since it is the strongest number this month and sets a positive tone for the page
A note that reach was down across the platform this month, with the inquiry numbers further down the page
Reach and impressions, which are bigger numbers than inquiries and easier to explain to a busy client

quiz.explanation: The report leads with the outcome the client's business feels, good or bad, then explains the cause and commits to three specific changes. Leading with followers in a month when inquiries fell is exactly the report a client stops trusting.

assignment.title: One Month of Social Media for a Real Business
assignment.brief_mdx: Pick a real Philippine small business you could plausibly work with — a milk tea shop, an online thrift seller, a dental clinic, a neighbourhood bakery, a Shopee reseller. Look at what they currently post. Then submit, as text, a complete month-one plan containing: (1) a short client brief — what they sell, who buys, what result they want from social media; (2) a brand voice brief you would paste into your AI prompts, including tone, Taglish preference and banned words; (3) four content pillars with a one-line reason each, plus your posting mix; (4) a two-week calendar table with date, platform, pillar, format and hook for every post; (5) one content idea written out fully as three finished captions — one Facebook, one Instagram or TikTok, one LinkedIn — with a line on what you changed for each and why; (6) three replies you would send from the inbox, including one to a public comment complaining about a late order; and (7) the three metrics you would report at month's end and what you would change because of them. Plain text or Markdown. No design work — the words are the deliverable.
criteria: Pillars and calendar come from this specific business's real offers and customer questions rather than generic categories, and every calendar row is tagged to a pillar
The three captions come from one idea but are genuinely rewritten per platform — different opening line, length, format and call to action — not the same caption pasted three times
Captions read like a person wrote them: concrete details about the business, a first line that says something specific, and no hollow AI filler or fake enthusiasm
The complaint reply de-escalates, offers a real next step, moves the right part of the conversation to DM, and promises nothing the manager is not authorised to promise
The reporting section names metrics tied to the client's business result rather than follower count, and states what would change next month because of them
The calendar is realistic to run: sustainable posting frequency, plausible dates and times for a PH audience, and specific enough that a client could approve it as-is
